newsitem.title: USA: Judge strips tobacco of key defense in Florida suit.
newsitem.headline: Judge strips tobacco of key defense in Florida suit.

text.p: A Florida judge ruled Wednesday that tobacco companies cannot use public knowledge of the dangers of smoking as a defence, stripping cigarette makers of a key defence two days before the trial of Florida's billion-dollar Medicaid lawsuit.

Lawyers for both sides said the ruling, issued by Palm Beach Circuit Judge Harold Cohen, would significantly impair the industry's ability to defend itself against the lawsuit, which seeks to recover the costs of treating smoking-related illnesses.
"It means they have no defences," said W.C. Gentry, a lawyer representing the state.
"By this ruling the only thing they can try to prove is that cigarettes don't cause disease, the product wasn't defective, that they couldn't make a safer cigarette," he said.
Jury selection in the widely watched lawsuit was scheduled to begin Friday, with testimony expected to start in early September.

The tobacco companies, arguing about the evidence that can be presented to the jury ultimately selected to hear the case, wanted to claim that the state should have to prove that Medicaid recipients were deceived as to the dangers of smoking in order to recover damages.
"If not, there can be no injury," Philip Morris attorney Peter Bleakley said.
He said Cohen's ruling "seriously impairs our ability to defend ourselves, here or elsewhere."
"The ruling is wrong," he said. "The plaintiffs should have the burden of proving what we did caused injury."
Bleakley said Cohen's ruling could be grounds for reversible error should the case go to an appeals court.
The ruling came on a motion made by the state to bar use of depositions taken from 25 Medicaid recipients who were interviewed about their Medicaid related injuries.
Cohen himself called the ruling one of the most important he had made in the case.
Earlier in a day of hearings meant to determine what evidence the jury will be allowed to consider, Cohen made other rulings detrimental to the industry's defences.

He said the companies would not be allowed to argue the so-called "premature death benefit" -- that Florida saved money in its Medicaid programme because smokers die earlier than non-smokers -- to mitigate potential damages.

In their motion to present evidence on the "premature death benefit," the tobacco companies said: "Because smokers die younger on average than non-smokers, the former receive smaller Social Security payments and experience a briefer period of eligibility for Medicare services than the latter."
"If smokers cost less than non-smokers, then the jury should hear about it," argued Murray Garnick, an attorney for Philip Morris Cos. Inc.
Gentry said the idea of a premature death benefit credit was "abhorrent to civilised society."
"They are asking for a credit for killing people early," he said.
Cohen also ruled that the companies cannot make an argument that Florida contributed to tobacco-related illness by failing to vigorously enforce laws against the sale of cigarettes to minors.

The tobacco companies had hoped to show evidence that Florida was partly to blame for such illnesses because it enforced laws barring gambling and alcohol consumption by minors but did little or nothing to halt the sale of cigarettes to children.
